title: PIPs Fail 70-90 Percent of the Time, Here's Why https://www.thebestleadershipnewsletter.com/p/pips-fail-heres-why-performance-improvement-plan
author: The Best Leadership Newsletter Ever
source: The Best Leadership Newsletter Ever (thebestleadershipnewsletter.com), August 17, 2026
summary: Drawing an extended analogy from his mother's work as a family therapist, where the 'secret patient' in a child's treatment is often the parent, the author argues that Performance Improvement Plans fail 70-90% of the time because they misdiagnose the manager's dysfunction as the employee's deficiency. The central case study, a composite client called Emily, illustrates the pattern precisely: she warned her manager three separate times about an unworkable deadline, was told to 'just figure it out,' made a reasonable scope trade-off that impacted a client, and was then formally documented as having 'missed deadlines and failed to take ownership.' The author walks through the standard list of five PIP triggers (missed expectations, poor quality, missed deadlines, lack of ownership, communication problems) and reframes each one as potentially reflecting an unaddressed managerial failure, such as unclear expectations or a manager who doesn't listen, rather than an employee skill gap. He notes that the four things a manager is supposed to do once a PIP starts, defining expectations, meeting regularly, coaching, and documenting progress, are simply the baseline behaviors of competent management, meaning a PIP often becomes the first moment real management occurs. The piece closes with a direct behavioral prescription: before writing a PIP, identify who the 'secret patient' actually is.
points: Reframes the therapeutic concept of a 'secret patient' (a child's presenting problem is often really the parent's dysfunction) as a diagnostic lens for Performance Improvement Plans, arguing PIPs frequently misattribute managerial failure to employee deficiency.

Cites the statistic that 70-90% of employees placed on a PIP either resign or are terminated, framing this failure rate as evidence the tool is treating the wrong root cause rather than working as designed.

Walks through a detailed case study (Emily) where an employee who warned her manager three times about an unworkable deadline was later documented for 'missing deadlines' after her manager told her to simply 'figure it out.'

Reframes all five standard PIP triggers (missed expectations, poor quality, missed deadlines, lack of ownership, communication problems) individually as potentially reflecting unclear direction or an unresponsive manager rather than an employee skill gap.

Notes that the four required steps once a PIP begins (define expectations, meet regularly, coach and mentor, document progress) are simply baseline competent management, meaning a PIP is often the first moment real management actually starts.
quotes: Kids get sent to therapy because 'something is wrong with them.' But most of the time, the kid isn't the problem. They're just the symptom. When treating a child, there's always a secret patient.
Somewhere between 70 and 90 percent of people who are put on a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) either resign or get fired.

She told me, with clear frustration, that she'd warned people about the untenable timeline three separate times. Her manager told her to 'just figure it out.' So she figured it out. To do that, she cut the scope of a project.

In order to help the person on a PIP, the manager has to do four things: Define expectations. Meet regularly. Coach and mentor. Document progress. That's not so much a remediation process as it is the expected behavior of a manager.
Next time you feel a need to put together a Performance Improvement Plan, I want you to do something else first. Don't ask what's wrong with the employee. Ask who the secret patient is.
